title: NASA's New Telescope Could See What Even James Webb Can't
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope is famous for taking jaw-dropping pictures of space. But there's a whole part of the universe it literally cannot see. Now NASA is working on a new telescope that can. It's called PRIMA — short for Probe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics. PRIMA would look at the cosmos in far-infrared light, which has longer wavelengths than what Webb can detect. Think of it like this: Webb sees some colors of invisible light, but PRIMA sees different ones — colors that show where water and other ingredients for planets are hiding in space. "We can't actually address these science questions with JWST," said Meredith MacGregor, an astronomer at Johns Hopkins University. The telescope itself is about 5.9 feet (1.8 meters) wide. It would launch no earlier than 2033 and run for five years. Its goals: figure out how planets form, how galaxies grow, and how black holes evolve. The cost? About $1.2 billion — way less than Webb's $10 billion price tag. PRIMA is the first of a new class called Probe Explorers, missions that sit between giant flagship projects and smaller ones. "I'm most excited about the things I don't yet know," said astronomer Alberto Bolatto. Same here.
why_it_matters: New telescopes like PRIMA will answer big questions about planets and space during your lifetime, and could show where the ingredients for worlds like ours are hiding.

background_read: The James Webb Space Telescope (a huge space telescope launched in 2021) studies infrared light — invisible 'colors' beyond red that our eyes cannot see.
NASA (the U.S. space agency that builds and launches space telescopes) is now planning PRIMA, which would look at far-infrared light.
Astronomers use many kinds of light — radio, infrared, visible, and X-rays — because each one shows different things hiding in space.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA, plus astronomers like Meredith MacGregor of Johns Hopkins University and Alberto Bolatto.
WHAT: NASA is working on PRIMA, a new telescope that would study far-infrared light the James Webb telescope cannot detect.
WHERE: It would launch into space no earlier than 2033 and run for five years.
WHY: To answer questions Webb cannot, such as how planets form, how galaxies grow, and how black holes change, and to find where water hides in space.

perspectives.description: They say PRIMA can see colors of light Webb cannot, so it can answer science questions nothing else can reach — and for far less money.
They point out that $1.2 billion is still a lot, and a launch planned for the 2030s could be delayed, so the wait may be long.
They are simply looking forward to new pictures and discoveries, and they like the idea that the best findings may be the ones nobody expects yet.
